questions.prompt: A report asks only about Clinic A. Which average should it use, and why?

content.title: minutes waited to see a nurse

content.text: A = Clinic A; B = Clinic B.

options.label: A
options.text: 9.5 minutes; it gives both group averages equal weight.

options.label: B
options.text: 12 minutes; it uses the higher group's values.

options.label: C
options.text: 7 minutes; it uses only A's four values.

options.label: D
options.text: 8.67 minutes; it uses all six values.

support.hint: The requested average is for Clinic A, so first decide which observations belong in that calculation.

stuck.introduction: Separate the group you need before calculating its mean.
steps: Identify all waiting-time observations recorded for Clinic A.
Add those observations and divide by the number of Clinic A observations.
Check the unit and choose the option whose calculation and explanation both match the requested population.

questions.prompt: Which statement fairly compares how often the groups got a checkup?

content.text: A = Clinic A; B = Clinic B.

options.label: A
options.text: B has the higher rate because 24 is more than 18.

options.label: B
options.text: A has a 28% rate and B has a 38% rate; use all 64 cases.

options.label: C
options.text: The rates are equal because both groups have successes.

options.label: D
options.text: A has the higher rate, 75% versus 60%, despite fewer successes.

support.hint: Different group sizes mean that success counts alone do not describe how often a checkup occurred.

stuck.introduction: Compare successes relative to each clinic's opportunities.
steps: For each clinic, identify the Met goal count and its own All cases total.
Calculate Met goal divided by All cases, then multiply by 100 for each clinic.
Compare those rates separately from the raw counts and select the statement consistent with both.

questions.skillLabel: Denominators and limits of percentage inference
questions.prompt: At a clinic, what can you find about people who did not join?

options.label: A
options.text: You need both group totals to find the share among nonmembers.

options.label: B
options.text: 6% of nonmembers are from Area A; subtract 42 from 48.

options.label: C
options.text: 90% of nonmembers are from Area A; add the two shares.

options.label: D
options.text: 42% of nonmembers are from Area A; use the eligible share.

support.hint: The two percentages describe different populations. Ask what totals you would need to isolate nonmembers.

stuck.introduction: Work backward from the population named in the question.
steps: Label the two populations: program members and everyone who could join.
To calculate a nonmember share, identify the counts needed for Area A nonmembers and for all nonmembers.
Check whether the table provides enough information to obtain those counts. Only subtract quantities that represent compatible counts or shares of the same total.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, which reading of the shares is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A is 6 points higher, so the program worked better in A.

options.label: B
options.text: B is 6 points higher and A is 6 points lower among members.

options.label: C
options.text: C must have the fewest eligible people because its share is 20%.

options.label: D
options.text: A is 6 points higher, B 6 lower, C equal; this does not show impact.

support.hint: Compare the same area's share across the two populations, and separate a participation pattern from a claim about impact.

stuck.introduction: Read each area as a comparison of two percentages.
steps: For each area, subtract its Could join percentage from its Members percentage.
Describe each result as higher, lower, or equal, using percentage points for the difference.
Check whether an option adds a claim about effectiveness or actual population counts that the table does not establish.

questions.prompt: Two sites count missed checkups. Which comparison is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The rates are 3% and 8%; the totals do not matter.

options.label: B
options.text: B has more events; A has the higher rate, 0.3% versus 0.2%.

options.label: C
options.text: B has more events and the higher rate because 8 is larger.

options.label: D
options.text: A has more events and the lower rate because 1,000 is smaller.

support.hint: A larger event count can accompany a smaller event rate when the totals differ.

stuck.introduction: Calculate the two rates before comparing the sites.
steps: Record each site's event count alongside its own total number of cases.
For each site, divide events by all cases and multiply by 100. Keep enough decimal places to represent a percentage below 1%.
Compare the raw counts and the percentages separately, then check both parts of each option.

questions.prompt: Compare monthly flu records. Both areas cover the same time period. Which comparison uses a fair population base?

options.label: A
options.text: B has the lower rate: 1.5 versus 2 per 1,000.

options.label: B
options.text: B has fewer events but a higher rate: 4.5 versus 3 per 1,000.

options.label: C
options.text: A has the higher rate because 240 is more than 180.

options.label: D
options.text: The rates are equal because both areas have thousands of people.

support.hint: Put both areas on the same population base before comparing their event rates.

stuck.introduction: Express the records as events per 1,000 people.
steps: Pair each area's event count with that area's population for the stated time period.
For each area, calculate events divided by people, then multiply by 1,000.
Label both results per 1,000 people and compare the rates separately from the total event counts.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, Yes means the case got a checkup. A worker uses 105 ÷ 300 for A's Yes rate. Which correction is right?

content.text: A = Clinic A; B = Clinic B.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep 105 ÷ 300 = 35%; all cases belong in a group rate.

options.label: B
options.text: Use 105 ÷ 185; only Yes cases belong in the total.

options.label: C
options.text: Use 105 ÷ 35; compare Yes with No to get the Yes percent.

options.label: D
options.text: Use 105 ÷ 140 = 75%; 105 ÷ 300 is a share of all cases.

support.hint: The phrase A's Yes rate tells you which cases belong in the denominator.

stuck.introduction: Name what the numerator and denominator each represent.
steps: Identify the Yes count for Clinic A.
Find all Clinic A cases by combining its Yes and No counts, then calculate A's Yes count divided by that total.
Multiply by 100 and compare this within-group percentage with a calculation that instead uses all cases from both clinics.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, Yes means the case got a checkup. No means the goal was not met. Which is a fair comparison?

content.text: A = Clinic A; B = Clinic B.

options.label: A
options.text: A 12% and B 27%; use all 300 cases for both groups.

options.label: B
options.text: A 30% and B 70%; use only the 115 No cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare only 35 with 80; different group sizes rule out rates.

options.label: D
options.text: A 25% and B 50%; rates allow comparison despite different sizes.

support.hint: For each group, compare the No count with all cases in that same group.

stuck.introduction: Use the same definition of unmet-goal rate for both clinics.
steps: Identify each clinic's No count and its own All cases total.
Divide No by All cases and multiply by 100 separately for A and B.
Compare the resulting percentages and check whether each option uses within-group totals consistently.

questions.skillLabel: Selecting a measure of center with an outlier
questions.prompt: A report needs a usual value for the minutes waited to see a nurse. Which choice fits the data?

options.label: A
options.text: Mean 10 minutes; the mean is always the middle value.

options.label: B
options.text: Median 10 minutes; 45 pulls the mean up to about 14.71.

options.label: C
options.text: Mean 14.71 minutes; one high value has no effect on it.

options.label: D
options.text: Median 14.71 minutes; it uses all values equally.

support.hint: Consider how an unusually large waiting time affects the mean compared with the middle observation.

stuck.introduction: Compare two ways of describing a usual waiting time.
steps: Put the waiting times in order and locate the middle observation.
Calculate the mean by adding all waiting times and dividing by the number of observations.
Compare the summaries with where most observations lie, and check how the unusually high value influences each summary.

questions.prompt: Both groups average 10. Which statement compares the spread in minutes waited to see a nurse?

content.title: minutes waited to see a nurse

content.text: A = Clinic A; B = Clinic B.

options.label: A
options.text: A is steadier: its range is 2 minutes, compared with B's 16.

options.label: B
options.text: B is steadier because its highest value is larger.

options.label: C
options.text: They are equally steady because their means are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: A has a larger range because its smallest value is larger.

support.hint: Equal means do not tell you whether the individual waiting times are equally close together.

stuck.introduction: Compare variability separately from the average.
steps: Find the smallest and largest waiting times in each group.
Calculate each group's range as largest minus smallest, keeping minutes as the unit.
Use those ranges and the distances from the shared mean to compare how steady the two groups are.
